Manifestation contre le massacre congola: Demonstration against the Congolese massacre in Montréal on February 24, 2024. Photo: Edouard Desroches
Le samedi 24 février, une centaine de pe: On Saturday, February 24, about a hundred people gathered in the streets of Montréal to protest the massacres civilians have endured in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since rebel groups resumed armed conflict in 2021. The Congolese community also denounced the silence of the international community.
Au point de rassemblement, près de la st: At the gathering point near McGill station, members of the Congolese community proudly wear the colours of the DRC flag as they wait for the start time. The wind is icy. Some warm their hands by blowing on them, others stamp their feet to fight the cold, but every face shows a palpable determination: to make their voices heard and to demand that the international community break its silence.
Au milieu de la foule grandissante, un h: In the middle of the growing crowd, a man in his sixties, wrapped in a Congolese flag, is live on Facebook. “We are not flies to be killed like this,” he declares solemnly, before continuing his speech in Lingala, one of the national languages of the Congo.
Depuis le milieu des années 1990, le Con: Since the mid-1990s, the Congo has been mired in a conflict involving several local and foreign armed groups as well as Congolese government forces, along with widespread violence. The main cause of the conflict is the extraction of mineral resources in the east of the country, notably by Uganda and above all Rwanda.
D'après des rapports de l'ONU, l<l1>e go: According to UN reports, <l1>the Rwandan government is involved in training and financing the March 23 Movement (M23</l1>), a rebel group active in the eastern Congo. The group is accused of taking part in smuggling and trafficking of natural resources, notably minerals. Kinshasa also claims that Rwanda exports Congolese minerals onto its own territory via the M23. In addition to its illicit activities, the militia is also accused of serious human rights violations against local populations.
Malgré les preuves avancées, Kigali nie: Despite the evidence presented, Kigali has denied any involvement since the start of the conflict, and <l1>in turn accuses Kinshasa of collusion with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR)</l1>, made up mainly of Rwandan Hutu rebels who fled to the DRC after the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994.
Selon les données les plus récentes du C: According to the most recent data from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), dating from 2008, 5.4 million Congolese have died since the start of the conflict. However, some researchers dispute this figure, estimating that it is actually much lower*. The UN also estimates that the population has been massively displaced, with close to seven million people displaced within the country.
Moïse Mayo lors de la manifestation cont: Moïse Mayo at the demonstration against the Congolese massacre in Montréal on February 24, 2024. Photo: Edouard Desroches
Moïse Mayo, directeur de l'association d: Moïse Mayo, director of the Liberal Party association in Saint-Jérôme*, is one of the organizers of the demonstration. During the march, we stay close to him to better understand the demonstrators’ demands. The man, wearing a yellow vest, points out that the conflict in the eastern Congo is often wrongly perceived as an ethnic confrontation. “This is not a question of ethnic wars, people need to understand that! There are 250 ethnic groups in the Congo, and we are able to live together. The primary reason for this war in the east of the country is the extraction of raw materials at lower prices from the Congo,” he explains with irritation.
Il est 14 heures lorsque les manifestant: It is 2 p.m. when the demonstrators sing the national anthem, marking the start of the march. Feet begin to move in a heavy silence, broken by the sound of the horns of the procession. Cars decorated with flags of the Congo, but also of Senegal and Chad, blend into the march, a sign of African solidarity in this quest for justice.
Au bout de quelques minutes, des voix s’: After a few minutes, voices rise. The demonstrators accuse Kigali, but also the international community, of complicity through its silence in the face of the ongoing armed conflicts. “Genocide* in the Congo!”, “Canada complicit!”, “United States complicit!”, “France, complicit!” they shout.
Devant la boutique Apple située sur la r: In front of the Apple store on Sainte-Catherine Street, the demonstrators make a first stop. The protest cries intensify. “Apple complicit!” they yell, pointing to the responsibility of the multinational in the suffering endured by Congolese people. “The phones you use are Congolese!” declares a woman’s voice, angrily. She adds: “Your phones are soaked in Congolese blood!”
Apple*, ainsi que des compagnies tels qu: Apple*, along with companies such as Microsoft, Google, Dell and Tesla, is accused by International Rights Advocates (IRA), a human rights organization, of having benefited from child labour in mines producing cobalt, tin and tungsten, collectively known as 3T. These metals are crucial to the manufacture of many electronic devices such as smartphones, tablets and electric cars.
« Le malheur du Congo est que 70% du cob: “The misfortune of the Congo is that 70% of the world’s cobalt is found in our country,” says Mr. Mayo. In front of the doors of the Apple store, a shrill cry rings out from the crowd, the Congolese “Yi,” a cry of humiliation that carries the weight of collective indignation.
L'Organisation mondiale du travail a qua: The World Labour Organization has described the methods used by several companies in the Kivu provinces toward their employees as “modern slavery.” Numerous NGOs have also raised concerns about the working conditions of children, who still make up a significant share of the local workforce. According to the latest UNICEF figures, from 2014, more than 40,000 children in the DRC work in the mines.
M. Mayo nous partage, visiblement révolt: Mr. Mayo shares with us, visibly outraged: “I can’t imagine my 4-year-old daughter being raped, nor can I imagine my wife being raped by several men in front of my children. These are atrocities that have no words.” Mr. Mayo is referring to the latest testimonies published by <l1>Amnesty International in February 2023.</l1> Dozens of women and girls in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo have testified to being raped by M23 rebel groups. Each testimony describes in detail the barbarity the survivors endured.

Alors que la foule se déplace vers l’amb: As the crowd moves toward the U.S. consulate, one woman’s voice stands out: “They don’t want to listen to our voices, they turn a deaf ear, because they’re all robbing us!” She continues, “What we mourn isn’t even our stolen land and wealth, but the millions of dead! The atrocities our compatriots suffer, the rapes, the massacres!”
À ses côtés, sa sœur prend la parole : «: Beside her, her sister speaks: “We have cried enough, we have cried too much, we are tired of crying. We simply want the genocide to stop, the killings to stop! That’s all we want.”
Sa sœur rebondit : « Pour le Congo on ne: Her sister picks up: “For the Congo they say nothing. Is Black skin worth nothing?” For this demonstrator, the international community’s “silence” is a matter of skin colour, but also of economic interests from which Western countries profit. “It’s a question of colour but also of plunder. Everyone helps themselves, it’s not normal. For the Congo no one speaks, are we worth nothing or what?” she exclaims, her eyes furious.
« La vie d’un congolais vaut-elle moins: “Is the life of a Congolese person worth less than that of a Ukrainian?”
M. Mayo déplore également le silence des: Mr. Mayo also deplores the silence of Canadian authorities in the face of the Congolese massacre. “Staying silent in a situation like this is also being complicit in what is happening.”
Pour lui, il ne s'agit pas d'une omissio: For him, this is not an omission on the part of the Canadian state, but a deliberate choice to keep quiet. “We send letters to MPs, to senators here, to Justin Trudeau’s office, we even send correspondence to the White House. Everyone knows, but the silence remains astonishing,” he says.
Moïse Mayo souligne le contraste entre l: Moïse Mayo points to the contrast between the substantial support given to Ukraine from the start of the war and the widespread forgetting of the Congo. “The high death toll in the Congo far exceeds that of Ukraine, and that’s what knocks me to the ground. Is the life of a Congolese person worth less than that of a Ukrainian?” he laments. For him, this is a “double standard” policy: “The Congo and Ukraine are both living the same situation, it’s a geopolitical war!”
« À quand les sanctions sur Paul Kagame: “When will sanctions be imposed on Paul Kagame and his regime? Why this lack of interest in him?” Mr. Mayo continues. “Russia was rightly sanctioned, but Rwanda not at all!”
Le Canada impuissant face aux conflits s: Is Canada powerless in the face of the conflicts in the DRC?
Patrick Mbeko, politologue canadien d'or: Patrick Mbeko, a Canadian political scientist of Congolese origin, is a specialist in the geopolitical issues of the African Great Lakes region. According to the expert, Canada does not have the necessary influence to intervene in the Congo’s geopolitical issues. “Canada is a minor player in what is happening in the eastern Congo. Even though we are a member of the G7, Canada doesn’t have enough leverage to tip the balance.” He also points out that Canada has no political ties with the Central African country.
Malgré le soutien du Canada à la mission: Despite Canada’s support for the United Nations Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mr. Mbeko highlights <l1>the partnership ties Canada maintains with Rwanda.</l1> “Supporting the UN and at the same time being an ally of Rwanda? It’s only to give yourself a clear conscience,” he says. He continues, “If Canada is to act, it should be by calling on Rwanda to show restraint. That might encourage the Rwandan authorities to reassess their stance on supporting the criminals operating in the eastern DRC.”
Affaires mondiales Canada affirme que le: Global Affairs Canada says the country is concerned about the recent escalation of hostilities in the eastern DRC. Canada also calls on Rwanda to end its support for armed groups in the region.
Alors que la foule poursuit sa marche su: As the crowd continues its march along Sainte-Catherine Street toward the French consulate, its last stop, Mr. Mayo takes the megaphone: “We will remain standing until the international community as a whole realizes that Congolese life has value.” The demonstrators chant “France complicit!” once again.
Le mardi 20 février, Paris dénonçait dan: On Tuesday, February 20, Paris denounced in a statement “the violations of territorial integrity” of the DRC and the violence against civilian populations in the east of the country. France notably called on Rwanda “to cease all support” to the M23 rebels and “to withdraw from Congolese territory.” The United States also “strongly” condemned “the escalation of violence caused by the actions of the M23 rebels, supported by Rwanda.”
Lors d'une séance parlementaire le jeudi: During a parliamentary session on Thursday, February 23, <l1>Raoul Hedebouw, head of the Workers’ Party of Belgium, denounced the inaction of Belgium and Western governments in the face of the Congolese massacre.</l1>
Le politicien a également pointé du doig: The politician also pointed the finger at the European Union, following its recent signing of an agreement with Rwanda on “the sustainable management of raw materials,” including resources such as coltan, cobalt, nickel, diamonds and copper. “Let’s be clear, diamonds don’t come from Rwanda. All of it comes from the eastern Congo,” Mr. Hedebouw said. “That is the reason Belgium doesn’t intervene: it’s business, it’s money,” he says.
À ce sujet, M. Mbeko estime que les pays: On this subject, Mr. Mbeko believes that European Union member countries are being hypocritical: “You cannot denounce the aggression against the Congo and sign a strategic partnership with a country that lives off the plunder of the Congo’s natural resources. Everyone knows where the Congo’s riches come from,” he maintains.
De retour au point de départ, les manife: Back at the starting point, the demonstrators sing the Congolese national anthem once more to close the march, this time with a symbolic gesture: one hand over the mouth and two fingers held like a gun at the temple.

*L’APLQ rassemble les partisans du Parti: *The APLQ brings together supporters of the Quebec Liberal Party, supports them in organizing their political actions and in obtaining backing.
*Le terme « génocide » est un terme suje: *The term “genocide” is subject to debate as a label for the massacres taking place in the eastern DRC. Some human rights groups and experts maintain that the events in the eastern Congo meet the criteria for genocide under international law. The “Mapping Project” report, published in 2010 by the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, documents the massive violence committed between 1993 and 2003, some of which is characterized as genocide. However, others dispute this characterization, preferring terms such as “crimes against humanity” or “war crimes.” To date, the International Criminal Court has not formally ruled on the question.
